heading: Let the habitat lead the journey
intro: An animal wish list is a useful starting point, but the proposed habitat deserves equal attention. Ask where the outings take place and how each location relates to your interests. A river outing and a forest walk offer different ways to observe. Choose a coherent regional program rather than a collection of distant stops built around promises of particular animals.
points: Ask for the actual base and excursion locations.
Compare the time spent observing with the time spent transferring.
Keep an alternative outing in mind if the original plan changes.

heading: Notice more than the headline species
intro: UNESCO records monkeys, sloths, tapirs and aquatic mammals in the Yasuní biosphere region. That record describes biodiversity, not the likelihood of meeting an animal on a short visit. Leave room for smaller discoveries and the guide’s interpretation. A photograph, distant movement or sound may begin an interesting explanation without becoming a close encounter or a certain species identification.
points: Ask which observations come from the proposed area, with dates and context.
Treat a target animal as an interest, never a booking guarantee.
Enjoy the surroundings even when a particular species stays out of view.

heading: Make interpretation part of the experience
intro: A guide can help you connect an observation with its setting and explain the limits of an identification. Tell the provider whether you prefer a broad introduction, photography or more detailed natural history. Ask how the outing works for your group and which languages are available. The best fit is a clear match between your interests and the actual person guiding.
points: Request the guide’s relevant regional experience and language.
Ask how uncertain identifications are explained to guests.
Discuss the balance between walking, stopping and listening.

heading: Give wildlife room
intro: Plan to observe from the route and position your guide permits. Do not feed, handle or pursue an animal for a closer photograph. A quiet pause can be part of the experience; it does not need to turn into an encounter arranged for the camera. Ask how the provider responds when wildlife approaches or when the group is asked to move away.
points: Ask for the wildlife observation rules before the outing.
Keep food and personal belongings managed as the guide directs.
Let the animal move away without following or blocking it.

heading: Plan for your own pace
intro: Describe your mobility, balance and camera needs before choosing an outing. Ask about trail surfaces, boarding, walking length and opportunities to pause; the destination name alone does not answer those questions. If a boat or other equipment is proposed, ask what is supplied and what you need to bring. Confirm arrangements for your booking rather than assume every property offers the same support.
points: Ask for an explanation of terrain and boarding requirements.
Clarify camera storage and rain protection without assuming provision.
Agree what alternatives are available for your group.

heading: Choose the program behind the photographs
intro: A wildlife gallery can show what someone photographed, but it cannot describe your future itinerary. Request a written plan with the base, responsible provider, included outings and transfers. Review current regional advice for every part of the journey, not only the reserve. A focused inquiry gives the provider something concrete to answer and makes competing proposals easier to compare.
points: Confirm days, nights and actual observation time in writing.
Ask what changes if an outing cannot take place.
Keep the proposal, terms and contact details together.
